title: Mira's Lord is Giridhar
hookLine: Mira's songs end on her own stamp, and every singer at a bhajan steps into a saint's love
carry: a bhajan sings in a saint's footsteps
last: BEFORE KRISHNA, THE SOUL IS THE BELOVED.

lines: CARRIED BY PEOPLE WHO LOVED THEM.
THE LAST LINE OF A SONG.
cards: This week, three women's voices. Shakuntala, told twice, in an epic and in a play. Andal refusing a mortal groom, questioning a conch, dreaming her wedding.

And Mira, dancing in bells and talking her way through a closed door. What reaches us of each one has been carried, retold, sung, by people who loved them. Mira's songs show it plainly, because they end with a signature.
To close the week, the last line of a Mira song.

teach.b: Listen to how a Mira song ends. Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the clever one who lifted the mountain.
The phrase comes back at the close of song after song sung in her name, like a seal pressed into wax.
Singers call that kind of closing name a chhap, a stamp. It tells you whose song it is. Now, how do these songs reach us?

By being sung: wandering singers, temple gatherings, women singing at home, families passing down the words they knew. And as they're sung, the same song can turn up in different words in different places.

So when a song ends with Mira's stamp, what it promises is a voice and a lineage, not a notarized author. That raises an honest question the songs can't settle: which lines go back to Mira's own lips?
Some readers sort the songs into older and newer.

Others say the question misses the point, since a song stays alive by being sung, changing a little in every mouth. Both views take her seriously. Last, the stamp teaches something about how Hindus pray in song.

teach.h: SATSANG: PRAYING IN A SAINT'S WORDS
teach.b: At a bhajan gathering, a satsang, the company of the good, nobody has to invent their own prayer. You borrow a saint's. Whoever sings Mira's song ends by stepping aside: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord.
For a few minutes each singer lends Mira a voice, and Mira lends them her love. That's how a woman who, tradition says, left a palace with almost nothing is still being sung.

how: Mira's songs are sung in bhajan gatherings, temples and concerts, and singers keep her name in the closing line.

games.q: you're a singer finishing one of Mira's songs. the last line comes. how do you end it?
o: with Mira's name: Mira's Lord is Giridhar.
games.why: the song ends with Mira's stamp. whoever sings it steps aside: not my Lord, but Mira's.

practice: Bring to mind one line of a prayer, hymn or song that someone else taught you.

Say it or hum it softly, and notice whose words it was before it was yours: the one who made it, and the people who carried it to you, the way singers carried Shakuntala, Andal and Mira this week. Then rest in the breath.
If you pray, give thanks for the saints whose words you borrow. If you don't, thank whoever carried them to you.

wordCard.voice: Mirabai. Her songs end with a stamp, Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and they've traveled from mouth to mouth, changing as they go.

orig.note: Hindi and Sanskrit: Giridhar, the one who holds up the mountain, a name of Krishna that seals Mira's songs.
